videos.subject: Your brain is costing you money
videos.script: Your brain is quietly costing you money. Not because you're bad with money, but because of how every human brain is wired. In one experiment, people paid more than double for the exact same tickets, just because of how they paid. In this video you'll see seven real psychology studies that show how your brain gets money wrong. And the last one shows the one way money reliably makes people happier. Let's start with that ticket experiment.
videos.hook_text: Your brain is costing you money

videos.subject: 1 · The pain of paying
videos.script: Researchers ran an auction for sold-out basketball tickets. The buyers were business students, people who know exactly what money is worth. Half were told they'd have to pay in cash. The other half were told they could pay by credit card. Same tickets, same seats, same game. The only difference was how the money would leave their hands. The card group bid more than twice as much. Psychologists call this the pain of paying. When you hand over cash, you see it and feel it leave. That small sting makes you stop and think. A card, or a tap with your phone, removes that sting. The money still leaves your account, but your brain barely registers it. Nobody is tricking you. Your brain simply feels payments instead of counting them. And when the feeling disappears, so does the brake. But what if a price you saw first could change what you think something is worth? That's the next study.

videos.subject: 2 · The anchor price
videos.script: Researchers asked experienced real estate agents to value a house. They toured it, saw the neighbourhood, and got the same information sheet. Except for one number: the listing price. Some agents saw a high listing price, others a low one. The agents who saw the higher price valued the very same house much higher. And most of them said the listing price hadn't influenced them at all. This is called anchoring. The first number your brain sees becomes a reference point, and everything after it gets judged against that number. That's why a jacket marked down from three hundred to one fifty feels like a bargain, even if you'd never have paid one fifty for it on its own. The first price you see isn't information. It's an anchor. And once it's dropped, it's hard to pull back up. Now here's a trick that uses a product nobody is supposed to buy.

videos.subject: 3 · The decoy
videos.script: Imagine a cinema. Small popcorn: three dollars. Large popcorn: seven dollars. Most people pick the small. Now the cinema adds a medium for six fifty. Suddenly the large looks like a steal, just fifty cents more than the medium, and more people buy the large. Nobody really wanted the medium. It was never meant to sell. It's a decoy. Researchers have shown this again and again: adding an option that is clearly worse makes the better option look much more attractive. Your brain struggles to judge value on its own. It's much easier to compare. So it compares whatever options are in front of it, even the ones placed there on purpose. Next time you see three options, ask yourself: if the middle one didn't exist, which would I choose? Halfway through, here's the study that changes how you think about losing money.

videos.subject: 4 · Mental accounting
videos.script: Imagine you've decided to see a play. The ticket costs ten dollars. As you arrive at the theatre, you discover you've lost a ten-dollar bill. Would you still buy a ticket? In the original study, eighty-eight percent said yes. Now imagine a different version. You bought the ticket in advance. At the door, you discover you've lost the ticket. Would you pay ten dollars for another one? This time, fewer than half said yes. In both cases, you're ten dollars poorer. It's the same loss. But your brain doesn't keep money in one big pot. It keeps it in separate little accounts. The lost bill comes out of a general cash account. The lost ticket comes out of the theatre account, and now the play seems to cost twenty. This is called mental accounting. It's why a tax refund feels like free money to spend, while the same amount from your salary feels carefully earned. A dollar is a dollar. But your brain labels every dollar by where it came from and what it's for.

videos.subject: 5 · Why you overvalue what you own
videos.script: Researchers gave coffee mugs to half the students in a class. The other half got nothing. Then they let them trade. Owners named the lowest price they'd accept. Buyers named the highest price they'd pay. If people valued mugs the same way, about half the mugs should have changed hands. Very few did. The owners wanted more than twice what the buyers would pay, for a mug they'd owned for just a few minutes. This is the endowment effect. The moment something becomes yours, giving it up feels like a loss. And losses hit your brain harder than gains. Studies suggest a loss feels roughly twice as strong as a gain of the same size. That's why free trials work so well. Once something is yours, cancelling feels like losing it. And it's why that box of stuff in your closet is so hard to throw away. The next study shows how your brain handles the future, and how a simple change helped people save almost four times more.
videos.hook_text: 5 · Why you overvalue what you own

videos.subject: 6 · Present bias
videos.script: Would you rather have a hundred dollars today, or a hundred and ten next week? Lots of people take the hundred today. But ask them: a hundred dollars in a year, or a hundred and ten in a year and a week? Now almost everyone waits the extra week. It's the same one-week wait for the same ten dollars. But when the reward is right now, your brain overvalues it. This is called present bias. Your brain treats your future self almost like a stranger. That's why saving feels so hard. Saving means giving something up now, for someone you've never met: future you. Two economists designed a program around this. Instead of asking employees to save more today, they asked them to commit to saving part of their future pay raises. Nothing was taken from today's paycheck, so present bias never kicked in. In the first company that tried it, average savings rates went from three and a half percent to almost fourteen percent in under four years. Same people, same incomes. The only change was when the decision hit. And the final study answers the question everyone asks: can money actually make you happier?

videos.subject: 7 · Money and happiness
videos.script: Researchers walked up to people in the morning and handed them an envelope with money. Five dollars for some, twenty for others. Half were told to spend it on themselves by the end of the day: a bill, a treat, something for themselves. The other half were told to spend it on someone else: a gift for a friend, or a donation to charity. In the evening, the researchers called everyone back and asked how happy they felt. The people who spent the money on others were happier. The amount didn't matter. How they spent it did. Before the study, most people predicted the opposite: that spending on themselves would make them happier, and that more money would help more. Both guesses were wrong. Other studies point the same way: spending on experiences and on other people tends to bring more lasting happiness than buying more things. So your brain may be bad at handling money. But it's very good at one thing: feeling good when that money connects you to other people. If that surprised you, watch this next: why your brain only remembers the worst part and the ending of everything you live through.
